title: DC motor: construction and torque
introduction: A DC motor turns electrical energy into rotation. Learn how its parts keep torque in one direction.

sections.heading: Construction
sections.body: The field system stays still. The armature rotates inside it. Brushes connect the supply to the rotating winding.

activities.title: Explore the construction map
activities.prompt: This schematic maps the parts and their functions. Select every part.

parts.label: Yoke
parts.description: The steel yoke supports the poles and provides a magnetic return path.

parts.label: Field winding
parts.description: Current in the field winding creates the stationary magnetic field.

parts.label: Armature
parts.description: The armature carries conductors that experience force in the magnetic field.

parts.label: Commutator
parts.description: Copper segments reverse current in each coil as it passes the neutral plane, maintaining the torque direction.

parts.label: Brushes
parts.description: Carbon brushes carry current between the stationary supply and the rotating commutator.

sections.heading: From back EMF to torque
sections.body: Let $P$ be poles, $\Phi$ flux per pole in Wb, $Z$ conductors, $A$ parallel paths, and $N$ speed in rpm. Armature current $I_a$ is in amperes. Neglect brush voltage drop and mechanical losses in this ideal model.

activities.title: Derive the torque equation
activities.prompt: Start with flux cutting, then connect induced EMF to converted mechanical power.

steps.heading: Rate of flux cutting
steps.explanation: A conductor cuts flux $P\Phi$ per revolution. One revolution takes $60/N$ seconds.

steps.heading: Conductors in series
steps.explanation: Each parallel path contains $Z/A$ series conductors. The armature EMF equals one path's EMF.

steps.heading: Converted power
steps.explanation: The electromagnetic power converted to rotation is $E_b I_a$. Rotational power is torque times angular speed.

steps.heading: Substitute and cancel speed
steps.explanation: Substitute the EMF and angular-speed expressions. The speed terms cancel, leaving torque in N m.

activities.title: Why use a commutator?
activities.prompt: What happens to a simple DC-fed coil connected through slip rings after it passes the neutral plane?
activities.hint: Consider which pole each side of the coil now faces.
activities.explanation: Torque reverses because the coil sides move under opposite poles while their current directions stay unchanged. The commutator reverses coil current to keep torque in one direction; it does not remove winding resistance.

sections.heading: Motor lab
sections.body: The armature voltage balance gives $E_b = V-I_a R_a$. This model neglects brush voltage drop and assumes fixed armature resistance.

activities.title: Predict the back EMF
activities.prompt: Predict what happens to back EMF when armature current increases at fixed voltage. Move the current slider to test it.
activities.explanation: Increasing current increases the resistive voltage drop, reducing back EMF at fixed supply voltage. Copper loss grows with current squared. The selected ranges keep back EMF positive; this ideal voltage-balance model does not predict transient speed.

activities.title: Calculate back EMF
activities.prompt: A motor has a 220 V supply, 10 A armature current and 0.5 ohm armature resistance. Neglect brush voltage drop. Find the back EMF in volts.

sections.heading: Exam practice
sections.body: Use this generated practice question to check your explanation and derivation. The rubric gives suggested practice marks.

activities.title: Construction and torque: long answer
activities.prompt: Explain the principal parts of a DC motor and derive its torque equation. State the assumptions used.
activities.solution:
1. The stationary field winding produces magnetic flux; the yoke supports the poles and provides the return path.
2. The rotating armature carries conductors; brushes supply it through commutator segments.
3. A conductor cuts $P\Phi$ flux in $60/N$ seconds; $Z/A$ conductors in series give $E_b=P\Phi ZN/(60A)$.
4. Use converted power $E_b I_a=T\omega$ and $\omega=2\pi N/60$ to obtain $T=PZ\Phi I_a/(2\pi A)$. This is electromagnetic torque; shaft torque is lower when mechanical losses are included.

rubric.criterion: Explain the field system, armature and their functions.
Explain brushes and the commutator's current reversal.
Derive back EMF from flux cutting and series conductors.
Use power and angular speed to derive torque; state assumptions.
